hints: Focus on what makes a bond covalent rather than ionic, sharing electrons versus transfer, and how polarising power can change the picture.
Ammonia is clearly a simple molecule with N-H shared pairs, while calcium fluoride is a classic Group 2 ionic lattice with no sharing.
Think about aluminium as a small, highly charged 3+ ion and how it distorts chloride electrons to give covalent character, then combine which two qualify.
walkthrough:
**Recall the covalent test**

Think sharing, not just metal plus non-metal. Covalent means electron pairs are shared between atoms, often in discrete molecules.

Rule of thumb:
$$\text{small, highly charged cation + large anion} \rightarrow \text{covalent character}$$

**Check 2 and 3 first**

Ammonia, $\text{NH}_3$, is non-metal plus non-metal with three N-H shared pairs, so definitely covalent. Calcium fluoride, $\text{CaF}_2$, is $\text{Ca}^{2+}$ with $\text{F}^-$, a low charge, large cation difference, so a typical ionic lattice with electron transfer and no covalent bonds.

**Decide the tricky one, aluminium chloride**

$\text{AlCl}_3$ looks ionic at first glance, but $\text{Al}^{3+}$ is very small and highly polarising. It pulls $\text{Cl}^-$ electron clouds towards itself so strongly that the bond becomes polar covalent, existing as $\text{Al}_2\text{Cl}_6$ molecules when covalent.

Conclusion: 1 and 2 contain covalent bonds, 3 does not.

options.A: Incorrect because it includes all three. Calcium fluoride is fully ionic with Ca2+ and F- ions, so it does not contain covalent bonds.
options.B: Correct because 1 and 2 only are right. Ammonia has N-H covalent bonds and aluminium chloride has polar covalent Al-Cl bonds due to polarisation by Al3+, while calcium fluoride is ionic.
options.C: Incorrect because it includes calcium fluoride and misses aluminium chloride. Calcium fluoride has no covalent character, and aluminium chloride does have covalent bonds.
options.D: Incorrect because it includes only 1. Ammonia must also be included as it is a classic covalent molecule with three shared N-H pairs and a lone pair.
